body:
India's best-documented frameworks translate the same ideas locally. Motilal Oswal's **QGLP** stands for Quality of business and management, Growth in earnings, Longevity of both, and a favourable Price ([Motilal Oswal PMS](https://pms.motilaloswalmf.com/about-us/investment-philosophy)). The 100x study added **S for Size** (SQGLP) and concluded that "the biggest wealth is created when growth and rerating combine" ([Wealth Creation Study](https://www.motilaloswal.com/site/rreports/HTML/635542588369519988/index.htm)). Marcellus's **Consistent Compounders** filter demands **revenue growth above 10% and ROCE above 15% in every one of 10 consecutive years**. That leaves about 25–35 names, which moat research narrows to 12–15 ([Marcellus newsletter](https://marcellus.in/newsletter/consistent-compounders/valuing-longevity-of-healthy-fundamentals/); [Marcellus FAQ](https://marcellus.in/faqs)). Its forensic model grades accounting quality on about 10–12 ratios drawn from Schilit's *Financial Shenanigans* ([Marcellus](https://marcellus.in/portfolio-management-services/marcellus-consistent-compounder-pms)). Vijay Kedia's **SMILE** means "Small in size, Medium in experience, Large in aspiration, Extra-large in market potential" ([Value Research](https://www.valueresearchonline.com/stories/54019/how-to-invest-like-vijay-kedia/)). Jhunjhunwala, Kacholia, Dolly Khanna and Porinju Veliyath published **no formal checklists**. Their "rules" are media readings of their portfolio disclosures, so treat any specific claim about them as unverified.

Professional fundamental shops add process rather than secret formulas. Tiger Management's bull/bear debates stress-tested every idea, and the Tiger Cubs kept the pitch-and-debate model ([Wall Street Prep](https://wallstreetprep.com/knowledge/tiger-cubs)). Gary Klein's **pre-mortem** assumes the investment has already failed and asks why. The underlying "prospective hindsight" research found a 30% improvement in identifying reasons for future outcomes ([Klein, HBR](https://wiki.duraspace.org/download/attachments/104563925/ProjectPremortem.pdf?api=v2)). Some folklore edges have faded. The spin-off premium found in 1965–88 data looks much weaker in later samples ([McConnell et al. 2001](https://business.purdue.edu/faculty/mcconnell/publications/spinoffs-ex-ante-2001-vol74.pdf)). Greenblatt's magic formula reportedly works about 3 calendar years in 4. Greenblatt argues it keeps working *because* most investors quit after one or two bad years ([GuruFocus](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/891031/joel-greenblatt-why-people-dont-stick-to-their-strategies)). Critics note weaker post-publication returns ([Hedge Fund Alpha](https://hedgefundalpha.com/strategies/has-the-magic-formula-lost-its-sparkle/)).

body: `insight:cyclical-pe-inversion` · confidence: unverified For metals, cement, commercial vehicles, specialty chemicals and capital goods, earnings swing far more than the business's value, so trailing P/E inverts the signal. At the bottom (FY16 steel, FY21 CVs, the 2015–16 metals bust), earnings are depressed or negative and P/E looks very high or meaningless. That was the time to buy, when the balance sheet could survive. At the top (steel in 2021–22, Tata Steel and JSW at 4–6x P/E on record spreads; capital goods in Jan 2008), P/E looks cheap because peak margins are in the denominator. Better tools: EV/EBITDA on mid-cycle (5–10 year average) margins; P/B for metals (0.7x trough against 2–2.5x peak); EV per tonne against replacement cost for cement; and watching the supply response, because capacity additions end shortage margins (transformers in 2025–26, specialty chemicals in 2022–24, Indian cement after each consolidation wave). Early signals of a top: margins well above the 10-year average, everyone announcing capex, inventory build in the channel, trade protection doing the work. Signs of a bottom: capacity closures, industry losses, balance-sheet repair, policy relief (safeguard duty) not yet in prices. **lesson:** Normalise earnings; the supply response is the cycle killer; low P/E at peak margin is a sell signal. **examples:** Steel 2021–22 (low P/E peak), CVs FY21 (high P/E trough), capital goods Jan 2008 peak took ~14 years to regain, specialty chemicals 2021 peak. Sources: [1](https://www.devdiscourse.com/article/business/4003265-tata-steel-reports-rs-5055-crore-net-profit-in-india-business-for-q2fy27) · [2](https://www.psuconnect.in/financial/jsw-steel-q2-results-record-production-sales-consolidated-pat-at-5-359-cr) · [3](https://www.icra.in/Research/ViewResearchReport/domestic-led-volume-recovery-supports-growth-global-overcapacity-caps-prices/7086) Links: about `theme:sector-metals-mining`, about `theme:sector-cement`, about `theme:sector-capital-goods-epc-td`, illustrates `insight:transformer-peak-2026`, illustrates `case_study:capital-goods-2007`

body:
1. **FY26 domestic T&D order inflow fell short everywhere.**
   - Skipper's FY26 inflow was 87% of the first guide and 95% of the restated one; it cited CEA holding back bids, ROW, and transformer and HVDC shortages.
   - KPIL's T&D inflow was 90% of FY25's level, and India T&D fell from ~INR 7,000 cr to ~4,500 cr as L1s slipped into FY27.
   - KEC's India T&D intake was ~-11% against +20% guided. That was worsened by a **company-specific** 15-month gap in PGCIL awards, after an analyst raised a bribery inquiry involving Power Grid officials (single-source; see KEC.md).
   - **Group-level inflow misses were partial (84-100% of guide), not collapses.** Order-inflow promises cluster in "partly" (median category delivery 50%). The user's hypothesis is confirmed, but the effect is modest: expect ~85-95% of a T&D inflow guide in a slow-tendering year, not a blow-out.
2. **Dates slip one to two quarters everywhere.**
   - Skipper: second 75k t block, five dates.
   - KEC: E-Beam plant, five dates; Karnataka solar, three dates; Afghanistan receipt, three quarters late.
   - KPIL: VEPL sale, two quarters late against the first date; Indore collections, two quarters late; JJM recovery.

   The capacity/capex category is the weakest for the sector (median 36%). A one-quarter haircut on any T&D date is the base case, not a red flag.
3. **JJM water receivables broke every recovery promise** at both companies with water exposure (KEC: dues ~INR 800-900 cr broadly unchanged from Mar-25 to Nov-26; KPIL: INR 1,427 -> 1,551 -> ~1,600 cr). Skipper's polymer segment was hit by the same JJM cuts. This is a government-payment problem, so promises that depend on it should be scored but discounted when comparing managements.
4. **The FY26-27 operating environment hurt everyone:** labour shortages (elections, LPG), the Middle East war in Q4FY26-Q2FY27 (KEC ~INR 300-400 cr of revenue deferred per quarter; KPIL ~200-250 cr in Q4FY26; Skipper export orders) and freight costs.
5. **Restating a target downward without saying so happens at all three.** Skipper and KEC did it nine times each; KPIL three times, but its outcomes still cleared the original bar. It is industry-normal. What differs is how far the outcome falls short.

body:
1. **The hard set is clean but small: 8 of 39 known traps caught, 0 of 62 winners rejected.** Every catch was a
   fraud case and came from the *judgment* fraud signals: H1a fake cash (Satyam: ~Rs 5,000 cr earning far below
   FD rates while borrowing, visible in FY08 accounts), H1b economics too good for the business (Vakrangee's
   ROCE ~40% in a kiosk franchise; Manpasand outgrowing Frooti; Cox & Kings' debt and receivables in an
   advance-paid business), H1c profits nobody outside can audit (Wirecard's third-party acquirers; Rajesh
   Exports' ~1% margin on Rs 2 lakh cr of gold), H5 group receivables (Gitanjali, ~33% of receivables), H4 SME
   pumps (circular). Leverage blow-ups (Jet, IL&FS, Future, Zee, Suzlon-2008, Unitech, SVB, Lehman, Evergrande,
   GE…) pass the hard set every time, as does DHFL (a fraud whose tell was ALM mismatch): **no hard rule addresses solvency**.
2. **H2 (auditor exit over disagreement) never fired before T: 0 of 41.** In every case it is in the record
   (Vakrangee, Manpasand, Reliance Capital, Ricoh, Super Micro, Byju's) the auditor left *after* the peak, usually
   mid-collapse. It's a sell signal, not a buy-side screen. Keep it as a non-overridable exit trigger, not as an
   entry gate that ever catches anything early.
3. **H2b broad (any auditor exit / restatement / regulator-found misstatement / delayed results in 5y)** added Yes
   Bank (RBI NPA divergence, disclosed 2017), Super Micro at its 2024 peak (8-K 4.02 Nov-2018) and Celsius at its
   2024 peak (4.02 Mar-2022, a stock-comp restatement unrelated to the bust: lucky). Cost: Super Micro at the start
   of its 17–30x run (Jan-2023). A rejection there was still right on net for anyone buying the peak, but wrong for
   a Jan-2023 buyer (even after −86%, ~3x from T).
4. **H3 'not cooperating' never fired (0/43) and H4 only on its own source cases.** No evidence for or against;
   both are cheap to keep as detector rules (tools/detectors already watch ratings).
5. **G1 pledge > 25% is the best single pre-T flag where data exists: 8 of 20 traps vs 2 of 13 winners**
   (BSE XBRL at T: Gitanjali 79%, IL&FS Transportation 98%, Gensol 63%, Cox & Kings 54%, Zee 46%, Future 44%,
   Reliance Capital 34%; Luckin founders' margin loans). The 2 winners: Apollo Hospitals 71% (L12 false alarm) and
   Suzlon 76% at Dec-2019 (then ~49x). Graded, not hard, is right: the misses on both sides are real.
6. **The cash-flow tests (F1, F1b, G2, G5) fire on winners at least as often as on traps.** F1 CFO/PAT < 0.7:
   traps 6/20, winners 8/24. G5 negative FCF: traps 9/23, winners 15/30. The winners caught are the L12 pattern —
   HAL (sovereign receivables), BSE and Mazagon (customer/clearing money and advances swinging CFO), Trent (store
   build-out), Netflix (content), Super Micro (inventory). Meanwhile the *best-disguised* frauds pass them:
   Vakrangee (CFO/PAT 0.75), Cox & Kings (2.7 — fabricated cash), PC Jeweller (0.96), Valeant (11.5), GE. Cash
   conversion is a reason to ask what the working capital is made of, never a verdict.
7. **G4 P/E > 50 is the only flag that sees busts coming (7 of 9 busts at their peaks) but it also hit Trent
   (155x, then 19x), Deepak Nitrite (~69x, then 12x), Kaynes (104x, then 10x) and DMart.** Valuation belongs to
   stage 5, not to stage 2.
8. **A blind, mechanical H1b proxy (ROCE > 40% or OPM +10 pp in 3 years) does not reproduce the judgment rule**:
   it fires mostly on loss-to-profit recoveries (Paytm, Jet, Future, IL&FS) and on winners (Caplin, Tata Elxsi, CDSL,
   Palantir, Tesla), and misses Vakrangee (ROCE 3y avg just under 40). "Too good for the business" needs a peer and
   unit-economics comparison, not a threshold.
